article--viewer_content"><div class="a-wrapper"><div class="content"><div class="text"><div class="html-chunk"><p dir="ltr"><span>Docker is the containerization platform that is used to package your application and all its dependencies together in the form of containers to make sure that your application works seamlessly in any environment which can be developed or tested or in production. Docker is a tool designed to make it easier to create, deploy, and run applications by using containers. </span></p><p dir="ltr"><span>Containerization is a form of OS-based virtualization.</span></p><ul><li value="1"><span>It creates multiple isolated virtual units called containers in the userspace.</span></li><li value="2"><span>All containers share the same host operating system kernel.</span></li><li value="3"><span>Isolation between containers is achieved using:</span></li><li value="4"><span>Namespaces (process, network, filesystem isolation)</span></li><li value="5"><span>Resource control mechanisms (CPU, memory limits)</span></li></ul><h3 id="virtualization-vs-containerization" style="text-align:left"><img src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141015/dockercycle1.png"/><br/><span>Virtualization vs. Containerization</span></h3><p dir="ltr"><span>To understand Docker, you must understand what came before it: Virtual Machines (VMs).</span></p><ul><li value="1"><b><strong>Virtual Machines (VMs):</strong></b><span> Virtualize the Hardware. Each VM runs a full Operating System (OS) on top of a Hypervisor. This is heavy; a VM can take up GBs of space and minutes to boot.</span></li><li value="2"><b><strong>Containers (Docker):</strong></b><span> Virtualize the Operating System. Containers share the host's OS kernel but keep applications isolated in "User Space." This is lightweight; containers take up MBs of space and boot in milliseconds.</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><img loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141119/vm-vs-container1.png"/></p><table><thead><tr><th style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Feature</strong></b></th><th style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Virtual Machines (VM)</strong></b></th><th style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Docker Containers</strong></b></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Isolation Level</strong></b></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Hardware (Heavy)</span></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>OS Level (Lightweight)</span></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Boot Time</strong></b></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Minutes</span></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Milliseconds</span></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Size</strong></b></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Gigabytes (GB)</span></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Megabytes (MB)</span></td></tr><tr><td style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Portability</strong></b></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>Low (Specific to Hypervisor)</span></td><td style="text-align: center;"><span>High (Runs anywhere Docker is installed)</span></td></tr></tbody></table><h2 id="docker-architecture" style="text-align:left"><span>Docker Architecture</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><span>Docker uses a </span><b><strong>Client-Server</strong></b><span> architecture. It is not just a single program, but a system of three parts talking to each other.</span></p><ol><li value="1"><b><strong>Docker Client:</strong></b><span> The command line tool (</span><code><span>docker</span></code><span>) that you type commands into.</span></li><li value="2"><b><strong>Docker Daemon (dockerd)</strong></b><span>: The background process running on the host that does the heavy lifting (building, running, and distributing containers).</span></li><li value="3"><b><strong>Docker Registry:</strong></b><span> A storage location for Docker Images (like Docker Hub).</span></li></ol><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>The Workflow:</strong></b></p><ul><li value="1"><span>You type docker build -> Client sends request to Daemon -> Daemon creates an Image.</span></li><li value="2"><span>You type docker run -> Client sends request to Daemon -> Daemon launches a Container.</span></li></ul><figure class="image"><img alt="docker_architecture" data-resized="true" height="400" loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp" srcset="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp 800w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-100.webp 100w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-200.webp 200w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-300.webp 300w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-660.webp 660w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-768.webp 768w" width="800"/><figcaption> </figcaption></figure><h2 id="components-of-docker" style="text-align:left"><span>Components of Docker</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><span>The main components of </span><b><strong>Docker </strong></b><span>include - Docker clients and servers, Docker images, Dockerfile, </span><a href="https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/what-is-docker-registry/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><b><strong>Docker Registries</strong></b></a><span>, and Docker containers. These components are explained in detail in the below section : </span></p><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>Docker Clients and Servers</strong></b><span>- Docker has a client-server architecture. The Docker Daemon/Server consists of all containers. The Docker Daemon/Server receives the request from the Docker client through CLI or REST APIs and thus processes the request accordingly. Docker client and Daemon can be present on the same host or different host. </span></p><p dir="ltr"><img loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141157/Dockerclientserver1.png"/></p><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>Docker Images</strong></b><span>- A Docker Image is a read-only, inert template that contains the application code, libraries, dependencies, tools, and other files needed for an application to run.</span></p><ul><li value="1"><b><strong>Key Concept: </strong></b><span>Layered Architecture Images are not monolithic blobs; they are built in Layers.</span></li><li value="2"><span>If you pull an image like nginx, you aren't downloading one big file. You are downloading multiple small layers (e.g., a layer for the OS, a layer for the Nginx software, a layer for config files).</span></li><li value="3"><b><strong>Immutability:</strong></b><span> Once an image is built, it cannot be changed. If you need to fix a bug, you don't "patch" the image; you modify the Dockerfile and build a new image</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>Docker File</strong></b><span> -A Dockerfile is a plain text file containing a sequential list of instructions (commands) that the Docker Daemon reads to automatically build an image. It is the "source code" of your infrastructure.</span><b><strong> </strong></b><span>Every line in a Dockerfile creates a new "layer" in the image. Docker reads the file from top to bottom.</span></p><ul><li value="1"><span>FROM: The starting point (e.g., FROM ubuntu:20.04). This is the foundation.</span></li><li value="2"><span>RUN: Executes commands during the build process (e.g., RUN apt-get install python3). This "bakes" software into the image.</span></li><li value="3"><span>COPY: Moves your actual code from your computer into the image.</span></li><li value="4"><span>CMD: The default command that runs when the container starts (e.g., CMD ["python", "app.py"]).</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>Docker Containers</strong></b><span>- A Container is a runnable instance of an image. It is the actual "living" process. When you start a container, Docker takes the read-only Image and adds a thin Read-Write (R/W) layer on top of it.</span></p><p dir="ltr"><b><strong>Key Concept: The R/W Layer</strong></b></p><ul><li value="1"><span>Because the Image is read-only, the Container needs a place to write data (logs, temp files, database entries).</span></li><li value="2"><span>Any changes made inside a running container (like creating a file) happen in this temporary top layer. If you delete the container, this layer is destroyed, but the underlying Image remains untouched.</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><img loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915151739/docker_flowchart-1024x640.png"/></p><h2 id="docker-compose" style="text-align:left"><span>Docker Compose</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><a href="https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/installation-of-docker-compose/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><span>Docker Compose</span></a><span> is a tool with which we can create a multi-container application. It makes it easier to configure and  run applications made up of multiple containers. </span></p><ul><li value="1"><span>Makes it easier to configure and run applications with multiple containers.</span></li><li value="2"><span>An application needing WordPress and MySQL can be started together using one file.</span></li><li value="3"><b><strong>YAML file definition:</strong></b><span> Multi-container applications are defined in a docker-compose.yml file.</span></li><li value="4"><b><strong>Foreground execution</strong></b><span>: Running docker-compose up starts the application in the foreground.</span></li><li value="5"><b><strong>Default file lookup</strong></b><span>: Docker Compose looks for docker-compose.yml in the current folder.</span></li><li value="6"><b><strong>Background execution</strong></b><span>: Adding the -d option (docker-compose up -d) starts the application in detached mode (background).</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><span> Creating a docker-compose. YAML file for WordPress application : </span></p><pre><span>#cat docker-compose.yaml</span><br/><span>version: ’2’</span><br/><span>services:</span><br/><span>db:</span><br/><span>image: mysql:5.7</span><br/><span>volumes:db_data:/var/lib/mysql</span><br/><span>restart: always</span><br/><span>environment:</span><br/><span>MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: WordPress</span><br/><span>MYSQL_DATABASE: WordPress</span><br/><span>MYSQL_USER: WordPress</span><br/><span>MYSQL_PASSWORD: WordPress</span><br/><span>WordPress:</span><br/><span>depends_on:</span><br/><span>- DB</span><br/><span>image: WordPress:latest</span><br/><span>ports:</span><br/><span>- "8000:80"</span><br/><span>restart: always</span><br/><span>environment:</span><br/><span>WORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db:3306</span><br/><br/><span>WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: wordpress</span><br/><span>volumes:</span><br/><span>db_data:</span></pre><p dir="ltr"><span>In this docker-compose. YAML file, we have the following ports section for the WordPress container, which means that we are going to map the host’s 8000 port with the container’s 80 port. So that host can access the application with its IP and port no. </span></p><h3 id="hosting-docker-applications-with-hostinger" style="text-align:left"><span>Hosting Docker Applications with Hostinger</span></h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: start;"><a href="https://www.hostg.xyz/aff_c?offer_id=545&aff_id=115172&url_id=6820" rel="nofollow noreferrer noopener" target="_blank"><b><strong>Hostinger</strong></b></a><span> provides Docker VPS hosting that makes it easier to deploy and manage containerized applications. Its Docker Manager allows users to deploy and manage Docker containers through a visual interface, while Docker Compose support makes it possible to manage multi-container applications from a single environment. This can be useful for developers deploying applications that require multiple services, such as a web application and database.</span></p><h2 id="docker-networks" style="text-align:left"><span>Docker Networks</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><span>When we create and run a container, Docker by itself assigns an IP address to it, by default. Most of the time, it is required to create and deploy Docker networks as per our needs. So, Docker let us design the network as per our requirements. There are three types of Docker networks- default networks, user-defined networks, and overlay networks. </span><br/><span> </span></p><p dir="ltr"><img loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915142620/docker_networks2.png"/></p><p dir="ltr"><br/><span>To get a list of all the default networks that Docker creates, we run the command shown below - </span><br/><span> </span></p><p dir="ltr"><img loading="lazy" src="https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190903231155/networkin21.png"/></p><p dir="ltr"><span>There are FOUR types of networks in Docker - </span><br/><span> </span></p><ul><li value="1"><b><strong>Bridged network</strong></b><span>: When a new Docker container is created without the –network argument, Docker by default connects the container with the bridge network. In bridged networks, all the containers in a single host can connect through their IP addresses. A Bridge network is created when the span of Docker hosts is one i.e. when all containers run on a single host. We need an overlay network to create a network that has a span of more than one Docker host.</span></li><li value="2"><b><strong>Host network</strong></b><span>: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=host argument it pushes the container into the host network stack where the Docker daemon is running. All interfaces of the host are accessible from the container which is assigned to the host network. UseCase: High-performance networking.</span></li><li value="3"><b><strong>None network</strong></b><span>: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=none argument it puts the Docker container in its network stack. So, in this none network, no IP addresses are assigned to the container, because of which they cannot communicate with each other. UseCase: High-security, offline batch jobs.</span></li><li value="4"><b><strong>Overlay:</strong></b><span> Used for multi-host networking (Swarm/Kubernetes).</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr"><span>We can assign any one of the networks to the Docker containers. The --network option of the 'docker run' command is used to assign a specific network to the container. </span></p><pre><span>$docker run --network ="network name"</span></pre><p dir="ltr"><span>To get detailed information about a particular network we use the command- </span></p><pre><span>$docker network inspect "network name"</span></pre><h2 id="advantages-of-docker-" style="text-align:left"><span>Advantages of Docker</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><span>Docker has become popular nowadays because of the benefits provided by Docker containers. The main advantages of Docker are: </span></p><ol><li value="1"><b><strong>Speed</strong></b><span> - The speed of Docker containers compared to a virtual machine is very fast. The time required to build a container is very fast because they are tiny and lightweight. Development, testing, and deployment can be done faster as containers are small. Containers can be pushed for testing once they have been built and then from there on to the production environment.</span></li><li value="2"><b><strong>Portability</strong></b><span> - The applications that are built inside docker containers are extremely portable. These portable applications can easily be moved anywhere as a single element and their performance also remains the same.</span></li><li value="3"><b><strong>Scalability</strong></b><span> - Docker has the ability that it can be deployed on several physical servers, data servers, and cloud platforms. It can also be run on every Linux machine. Containers can easily be moved from a cloud environment to a local host and from there back to the cloud again at a fast pace.</span></li><li value="4"><b><strong>Density</strong></b><span> - Docker uses the resources that are available more efficiently because it does not use a hypervisor. This is the reason that more containers can be run on a single host as compared to virtual machines. Docker Containers have higher performance because of their high density and no overhead wastage of resources.</span></li></ol><h2 id="essential-docker-commands" style="text-align:left"><span>Essential Docker Commands</span></h2><p dir="ltr"><span>Here are the commands you will use most of the time:</span></p><table><thead><tr><th style="text-align: center;"><b><strong>Command</strong></b></th><th These components are explained in detail in the below section : \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Clients and Servers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- Docker has a client-server architecture. The Docker Daemon/Server consists of all containers. The Docker Daemon/Server receives the request from the Docker client through CLI or REST APIs and thus processes the request accordingly. Docker client and Daemon can be present on the same host or different host. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141157/Dockerclientserver1.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Images\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Docker Image is a read-only, inert template that contains the application code, libraries, dependencies, tools, and other files needed for an application to run.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLayered Architecture Images are not monolithic blobs; they are built in Layers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIf you pull an image like nginx, you aren't downloading one big file. You are downloading multiple small layers (e.g., a layer for the OS, a layer for the Nginx software, a layer for config files).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eImmutability:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Once an image is built, it cannot be changed. If you need to fix a bug, you don't \"patch\" the image; you modify the Dockerfile and build a new image\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker File\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e -A Dockerfile is a plain text file containing a sequential list of instructions (commands) that the Docker Daemon reads to automatically build an image. It is the \"source code\" of your infrastructure.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eEvery line in a Dockerfile creates a new \"layer\" in the image. Docker reads the file from top to bottom.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eFROM: The starting point (e.g., FROM ubuntu:20.04). This is the foundation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eRUN: Executes commands during the build process (e.g., RUN apt-get install python3). This \"bakes\" software into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCOPY: Moves your actual code from your computer into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCMD: The default command that runs when the container starts (e.g., CMD [\"python\", \"app.py\"]).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Containers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Container is a runnable instance of an image. It is the actual \"living\" process. When you start a container, Docker takes the read-only Image and adds a thin Read-Write (R/W) layer on top of it.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: The R/W Layer\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eBecause the Image is read-only, the Container needs a place to write data (logs, temp files, database entries).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAny changes made inside a running container (like creating a file) happen in this temporary top layer. If you delete the container, this layer is destroyed, but the underlying Image remains untouched.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915151739/docker_flowchart-1024x640.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-compose\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/installation-of-docker-compose/\" rel=\"noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e is a tool with which we can create a multi-container application. It makes it easier to configure and  run applications made up of multiple containers. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMakes it easier to configure and run applications with multiple containers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAn application needing WordPress and MySQL can be started together using one file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eYAML file definition:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Multi-container applications are defined in a docker-compose.yml file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eForeground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Running docker-compose up starts the application in the foreground.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"5\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDefault file lookup\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Docker Compose looks for docker-compose.yml in the current folder.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"6\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBackground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Adding the -d option (docker-compose up -d) starts the application in detached mode (background).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Creating a docker-compose. This can be useful for developers deploying applications that require multiple services, such as a web application and database.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-networks\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Networks\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen we create and run a container, Docker by itself assigns an IP address to it, by default. Most of the time, it is required to create and deploy Docker networks as per our needs. So, Docker let us design the network as per our requirements. There are three types of Docker networks- default networks, user-defined networks, and overlay networks. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915142620/docker_networks2.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTo get a list of all the default networks that Docker creates, we run the command shown below - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190903231155/networkin21.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThere are FOUR types of networks in Docker - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBridged network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created without the –network argument, Docker by default connects the container with the bridge network. In bridged networks, all the containers in a single host can connect through their IP addresses. A Bridge network is created when the span of Docker hosts is one i.e. when all containers run on a single host. We need an overlay network to create a network that has a span of more than one Docker host.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHost network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=host argument it pushes the container into the host network stack where the Docker daemon is running. All interfaces of the host are accessible from the container which is assigned to the host network. UseCase: High-performance networking.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNone network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=none argument it puts the Docker container in its network stack. So, in this none network, no IP addresses are assigned to the container, because of which they cannot communicate with each other. UseCase: High-security, offline batch jobs.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOverlay:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Used for multi-host networking (Swarm/Kubernetes).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can assign any one of the networks to the Docker containers. The main advantages of Docker are: \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSpeed\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - The speed of Docker containers compared to a virtual machine is very fast. The time required to build a container is very fast because they are tiny and lightweight. Development, testing, and deployment can be done faster as containers are small. Containers can be pushed for testing once they have been built and then from there on to the production environment.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePortability\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - The applications that are built inside docker containers are extremely portable. These portable applications can easily be moved anywhere as a single element and their performance also remains the same.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eScalability\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - Docker has the ability that it can be deployed on several physical servers, data servers, and cloud platforms. It can also be run on every Linux machine. Containers can easily be moved from a cloud environment to a local host and from there back to the cloud again at a fast pace.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDensity\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - Docker uses the resources that are available more efficiently because it does not use a hypervisor. This is the reason that more containers can be run on a single host as compared to virtual machines. Client sends request to Daemon -\u0026gt; Daemon creates an Image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eYou type docker run -\u0026gt; Client sends request to Daemon -\u0026gt; Daemon launches a Container.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image\"\u003e\u003cimg alt=\"docker_architecture\" data-resized=\"true\" height=\"400\" loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp\" srcset=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp 800w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-100.webp 100w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-200.webp 200w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-300.webp 300w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-660.webp 660w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-768.webp 768w\" width=\"800\"/\u003e\u003cfigcaption\u003e \u003c/figcaption\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"components-of-docker\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eComponents of Docker\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe main components of \u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003einclude - Docker clients and servers, Docker images, Dockerfile, \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/what-is-docker-registry/\" rel=\"noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Registries\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, and Docker containers. These components are explained in detail in the below section : \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Clients and Servers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- Docker has a client-server architecture. The Docker Daemon/Server consists of all containers. The Docker Daemon/Server receives the request from the Docker client through CLI or REST APIs and thus processes the request accordingly. Docker client and Daemon can be present on the same host or different host. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141157/Dockerclientserver1.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Images\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Docker Image is a read-only, inert template that contains the application code, libraries, dependencies, tools, and other files needed for an application to run.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLayered Architecture Images are not monolithic blobs; they are built in Layers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIf you pull an image like nginx, you aren't downloading one big file. You are downloading multiple small layers (e.g., a layer for the OS, a layer for the Nginx software, a layer for config files).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eImmutability:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Once an image is built, it cannot be changed. If you need to fix a bug, you don't \"patch\" the image; you modify the Dockerfile and build a new image\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker File\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e -A Dockerfile is a plain text file containing a sequential list of instructions (commands) that the Docker Daemon reads to automatically build an image. It is the \"source code\" of your infrastructure.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eEvery line in a Dockerfile creates a new \"layer\" in the image. Docker reads the file from top to bottom.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eFROM: The starting point (e.g., FROM ubuntu:20.04). This is the foundation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eRUN: Executes commands during the build process (e.g., RUN apt-get install python3). This \"bakes\" software into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCOPY: Moves your actual code from your computer into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCMD: The default command that runs when the container starts (e.g., CMD [\"python\", \"app.py\"]).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Containers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Container is a runnable instance of an image. It is the actual \"living\" process. When you start a container, Docker takes the read-only Image and adds a thin Read-Write (R/W) layer on top of it.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: The R/W Layer\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eBecause the Image is read-only, the Container needs a place to write data (logs, temp files, database entries).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAny changes made inside a running container (like creating a file) happen in this temporary top layer. If you delete the container, this layer is destroyed, but the underlying Image remains untouched.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915151739/docker_flowchart-1024x640.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-compose\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/installation-of-docker-compose/\" rel=\"noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e is a tool with which we can create a multi-container application. It makes it easier to configure and  run applications made up of multiple containers. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMakes it easier to configure and run applications with multiple containers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAn application needing WordPress and MySQL can be started together using one file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eYAML file definition:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Multi-container applications are defined in a docker-compose.yml file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eForeground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Running docker-compose up starts the application in the foreground.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"5\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDefault file lookup\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Docker Compose looks for docker-compose.yml in the current folder.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"6\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBackground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Adding the -d option (docker-compose up -d) starts the application in detached mode (background).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Creating a docker-compose. YAML file for WordPress application : \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cpre\u003e\u003cspan\u003e#cat docker-compose.yaml\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eversion: ’2’\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eservices:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edb:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eimage: mysql:5.7\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003evolumes:db_data:/var/lib/mysql\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003erestart: always\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eenvironment:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_DATABASE: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_USER: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_PASSWORD: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWordPress:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edepends_on:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- DB\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eimage: WordPress:latest\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eports:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- \"8000:80\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003erestart: always\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eenvironment:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db:3306\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: wordpress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003evolumes:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edb_data:\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn this docker-compose. YAML file, we have the following ports section for the WordPress container, which means that we are going to map the host’s 8000 port with the container’s 80 port. So that host can access the application with its IP and port no. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"hosting-docker-applications-with-hostinger\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eHosting Docker Applications with Hostinger\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\" style=\"text-align: start;\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.hostg.xyz/aff_c?offer_id=545\u0026amp;aff_id=115172\u0026amp;url_id=6820\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHostinger\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e provides Docker VPS hosting that makes it easier to deploy and manage containerized applications. Its Docker Manager allows users to deploy and manage Docker containers through a visual interface, while Docker Compose support makes it possible to manage multi-container applications from a single environment. This can be useful for developers deploying applications that require multiple services, such as a web application and database.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-networks\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Networks\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen we create and run a container, Docker by itself assigns an IP address to it, by default. Most of the time, it is required to create and deploy Docker networks as per our needs. So, Docker let us design the network as per our requirements. There are three types of Docker networks- default networks, user-defined networks, and overlay networks. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915142620/docker_networks2.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTo get a list of all the default networks that Docker creates, we run the command shown below - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190903231155/networkin21.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThere are FOUR types of networks in Docker - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBridged network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created without the –network argument, Docker by default connects the container with the bridge network. In bridged networks, all the containers in a single host can connect through their IP addresses. A Bridge network is created when the span of Docker hosts is one i.e. when all containers run on a single host. We need an overlay network to create a network that has a span of more than one Docker host.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHost network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=host argument it pushes the container into the host network stack where the Docker daemon is running. All interfaces of the host are accessible from the container which is assigned to the host network. UseCase: High-performance networking.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNone network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=none argument it puts the Docker container in its network stack. So, in this none network, no IP addresses are assigned to the container, because of which they cannot communicate with each other. UseCase: High-security, offline batch jobs.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOverlay:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Used for multi-host networking (Swarm/Kubernetes).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can assign any one of the networks to the Docker containers. The --network option of the 'docker run' command is used to assign a specific network to the container. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cpre\u003e\u003cspan\u003e$docker run --network =\"network name\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTo get detailed information about a particular network we use the command- \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cpre\u003e\u003cspan\u003e$docker network inspect \"network name\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"advantages-of-docker-\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAdvantages of Docker\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker has become popular nowadays because of the benefits provided by Docker containers. The main advantages of Docker are: \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSpeed\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - The speed of Docker containers compared to a virtual machine is very fast. The time required to build a container is very fast because they are tiny and lightweight. Development, testing, and deployment can be done faster as containers are small. Containers can be pushed for testing once they have been built and then from there on to the production environment.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePortability\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - The applications that are built inside docker containers are extremely portable. These portable applications can easily be moved anywhere as a single element and their performance also remains the same.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eScalability\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - Docker has the ability that it can be deployed on several physical servers, data servers, and cloud platforms. It can also be run on every Linux machine. Containers can easily be moved from a cloud environment to a local host and from there back to the cloud again at a fast pace.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDensity\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e - Docker uses the resources that are available more efficiently because it does not use a hypervisor. This is the reason that more containers can be run on a single host as compared to virtual machines. Docker Containers have higher performance because of their high density and no overhead wastage of resources.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"essential-docker-commands\" Docker is a tool designed to make it easier to create, deploy, and run applications by using containers. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eContainerization is a form of OS-based virtualization.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIt creates multiple isolated virtual units called containers in the userspace.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAll containers share the same host operating system kernel.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIsolation between containers is achieved using:\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eNamespaces (process, network, filesystem isolation)\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"5\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eResource control mechanisms (CPU, memory limits)\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"virtualization-vs-containerization\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141015/dockercycle1.png\"/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eVirtualization vs. Containerization\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTo understand Docker, you must understand what came before it: Virtual Machines (VMs).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eVirtual Machines (VMs):\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Virtualize the Hardware. Each VM runs a full Operating System (OS) on top of a Hypervisor. This is heavy; a VM can take up GBs of space and minutes to boot.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eContainers (Docker):\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Virtualize the Operating System. Containers share the host's OS kernel but keep applications isolated in \"User Space.\" This is lightweight; containers take up MBs of space and boot in milliseconds.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" Architecture\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker uses a \u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eClient-Server\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e architecture. It is not just a single program, but a system of three parts talking to each other.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Client:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e The command line tool (\u003c/span\u003e\u003ccode\u003e\u003cspan\u003edocker\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/code\u003e\u003cspan\u003e) that you type commands into.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Daemon (dockerd)\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: The background process running on the host that does the heavy lifting (building, running, and distributing containers).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Registry:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e A storage location for Docker Images (like Docker Hub).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe Workflow:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eYou type docker build -\u0026gt; Client sends request to Daemon -\u0026gt; Daemon creates an Image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eYou type docker run -\u0026gt; Client sends request to Daemon -\u0026gt; Daemon launches a Container.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cfigure class=\"image\"\u003e\u003cimg alt=\"docker_architecture\" data-resized=\"true\" height=\"400\" loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp\" srcset=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture.webp 800w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-100.webp 100w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-200.webp 200w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-300.webp 300w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-660.webp 660w,https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20260114153314494879/docker_architecture-768.webp 768w\" width=\"800\"/\u003e\u003cfigcaption\u003e \u003c/figcaption\u003e\u003c/figure\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"components-of-docker\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eComponents of Docker\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThe main components of \u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003einclude - Docker clients and servers, Docker images, Dockerfile, \u003c/span\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/what-is-docker-registry/\" rel=\"noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Registries\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e, and Docker containers. These components are explained in detail in the below section : \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Clients and Servers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- Docker has a client-server architecture. The Docker Daemon/Server consists of all containers. The Docker Daemon/Server receives the request from the Docker client through CLI or REST APIs and thus processes the request accordingly. Docker client and Daemon can be present on the same host or different host. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915141157/Dockerclientserver1.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Images\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Docker Image is a read-only, inert template that contains the application code, libraries, dependencies, tools, and other files needed for an application to run.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eLayered Architecture Images are not monolithic blobs; they are built in Layers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIf you pull an image like nginx, you aren't downloading one big file. You are downloading multiple small layers (e.g., a layer for the OS, a layer for the Nginx software, a layer for config files).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eImmutability:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Once an image is built, it cannot be changed. If you need to fix a bug, you don't \"patch\" the image; you modify the Dockerfile and build a new image\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker File\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e -A Dockerfile is a plain text file containing a sequential list of instructions (commands) that the Docker Daemon reads to automatically build an image. It is the \"source code\" of your infrastructure.\u003c/span\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003eEvery line in a Dockerfile creates a new \"layer\" in the image. Docker reads the file from top to bottom.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eFROM: The starting point (e.g., FROM ubuntu:20.04). This is the foundation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eRUN: Executes commands during the build process (e.g., RUN apt-get install python3). This \"bakes\" software into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCOPY: Moves your actual code from your computer into the image.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eCMD: The default command that runs when the container starts (e.g., CMD [\"python\", \"app.py\"]).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDocker Containers\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- A Container is a runnable instance of an image. It is the actual \"living\" process. When you start a container, Docker takes the read-only Image and adds a thin Read-Write (R/W) layer on top of it.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eKey Concept: The R/W Layer\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eBecause the Image is read-only, the Container needs a place to write data (logs, temp files, database entries).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAny changes made inside a running container (like creating a file) happen in this temporary top layer. If you delete the container, this layer is destroyed, but the underlying Image remains untouched.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915151739/docker_flowchart-1024x640.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-compose\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/devops/installation-of-docker-compose/\" rel=\"noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Compose\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e is a tool with which we can create a multi-container application. It makes it easier to configure and  run applications made up of multiple containers. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMakes it easier to configure and run applications with multiple containers.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eAn application needing WordPress and MySQL can be started together using one file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eYAML file definition:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Multi-container applications are defined in a docker-compose.yml file.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eForeground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Running docker-compose up starts the application in the foreground.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"5\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDefault file lookup\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Docker Compose looks for docker-compose.yml in the current folder.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"6\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBackground execution\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: Adding the -d option (docker-compose up -d) starts the application in detached mode (background).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Creating a docker-compose. YAML file for WordPress application : \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cpre\u003e\u003cspan\u003e#cat docker-compose.yaml\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eversion: ’2’\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eservices:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edb:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eimage: mysql:5.7\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003evolumes:db_data:/var/lib/mysql\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003erestart: always\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eenvironment:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_DATABASE: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_USER: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eMYSQL_PASSWORD: WordPress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWordPress:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edepends_on:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- DB\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eimage: WordPress:latest\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eports:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e- \"8000:80\"\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003erestart: always\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eenvironment:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db:3306\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: wordpress\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003evolumes:\u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003edb_data:\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eIn this docker-compose. YAML file, we have the following ports section for the WordPress container, which means that we are going to map the host’s 8000 port with the container’s 80 port. So that host can access the application with its IP and port no. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"hosting-docker-applications-with-hostinger\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eHosting Docker Applications with Hostinger\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\" style=\"text-align: start;\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.hostg.xyz/aff_c?offer_id=545\u0026amp;aff_id=115172\u0026amp;url_id=6820\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer noopener\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHostinger\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003cspan\u003e provides Docker VPS hosting that makes it easier to deploy and manage containerized applications. Its Docker Manager allows users to deploy and manage Docker containers through a visual interface, while Docker Compose support makes it possible to manage multi-container applications from a single environment. This can be useful for developers deploying applications that require multiple services, such as a web application and database.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch2 id=\"docker-networks\" style=\"text-align:left\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eDocker Networks\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWhen we create and run a container, Docker by itself assigns an IP address to it, by default. Most of the time, it is required to create and deploy Docker networks as per our needs. So, Docker let us design the network as per our requirements. There are three types of Docker networks- default networks, user-defined networks, and overlay networks. \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190915142620/docker_networks2.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003eTo get a list of all the default networks that Docker creates, we run the command shown below - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" src=\"https://media.geeksforgeeks.org/wp-content/uploads/20190903231155/networkin21.png\"/\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eThere are FOUR types of networks in Docker - \u003c/span\u003e\u003cbr/\u003e\u003cspan\u003e \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\u003cli value=\"1\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eBridged network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created without the –network argument, Docker by default connects the container with the bridge network. In bridged networks, all the containers in a single host can connect through their IP addresses. A Bridge network is created when the span of Docker hosts is one i.e. when all containers run on a single host. We need an overlay network to create a network that has a span of more than one Docker host.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"2\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHost network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=host argument it pushes the container into the host network stack where the Docker daemon is running. All interfaces of the host are accessible from the container which is assigned to the host network. UseCase: High-performance networking.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"3\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eNone network\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e: When a new Docker container is created with the –network=none argument it puts the Docker container in its network stack. So, in this none network, no IP addresses are assigned to the container, because of which they cannot communicate with each other. UseCase: High-security, offline batch jobs.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli value=\"4\"\u003e\u003cb\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOverlay:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/b\u003e\u003cspan\u003e Used for multi-host networking (Swarm/Kubernetes).\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp dir=\"ltr\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eWe can assign any one of the networks to the Docker containers.
